gradeK.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
gradeK.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Light and Shadows breakout. Use a flashlight to make shadows, change their size, and make a shadow puppet.
gradeK.footer: Kindergarten Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
gradeK.p.0: Can you make a shadow — and change it? Use a flashlight and your hands or a paper shape to make shadows on the wall. Then make them bigger and smaller!
gradeK.p.1: What did you need to make a shadow?
gradeK.p.2: How did you make the shadow bigger? (Try the words light and shadow.)
gradeK.li.1: A blank wall or a white paper "screen"
gradeK.li.2: Your hands, and a paper shape on a craft stick to make a puppet
gradeK.li.3: Ask: How can I make a shadow on the wall?
gradeK.li.4: Try: Shine the flashlight at the wall. Put your hand in the way — a shadow!
gradeK.li.5: Change it: Move your hand closer to the light. Does the shadow get bigger or smaller?
gradeK.li.6: Build: Make a shadow puppet from a paper shape on a stick.
gradeK.li.7: Show: Put on a little shadow show for a friend.
gradeK.li.8: Talk: What did you need to make the shadow?
gradeK.teks.0: (Kindergarten idea: light helps us see, and blocking it makes shadows.)

grade1.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade1.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Push, Pull, and Play! breakout. Build a ramp and use a push to send a toy car as far as you can — then make it even better.
grade1.footer: Grade 1 Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade1.p.0: Make a ramp that helps a toy car roll far. Let the car go from the top and see how far it rolls. Then change your ramp to make the car go even farther!
grade1.p.1: Which ramp made the car roll farther?
grade1.p.2: Why do you think so? (Try the words push, ramp, and far.)
grade1.li.0: A toy car or a ball that rolls
grade1.li.1: Something to make a ramp: a book, a board, or a piece of cardboard
grade1.li.2: Blocks or books to lift the top of the ramp up
grade1.li.3: A way to measure: floor tiles, big steps, or a measuring tape
grade1.li.4: Ask: How can I make the car roll far?
grade1.li.5: Imagine: Should the ramp be high or low? Take a guess!
grade1.li.6: Plan: Pick your ramp and how high to lift it.
grade1.li.7: Build: Set up your ramp. Let the car go from the top (no pushing — let gravity pull it!).
grade1.li.8: Test: Measure how far the car rolled. Write it down.
grade1.li.9: Make it better: Change one thing — make the ramp higher — and test again.
grade1.teks.0: (Grade 1 scientists to meet: Katherine Johnson, Sally Ride, Ernest Just.)

grade2.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade2.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Make Some Noise! breakout. Build a cup-and-string phone and send your voice across the room using sound — then make it work even better.
grade2.footer: Grade 2 Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade2.p.0: How can you talk to a friend far away without shouting? Build a string phone that carries your voice along a string using sound. The string vibrates and carries the sound to the other cup!
grade2.p.1: Did the string phone work better loose or tight?
grade2.p.2: Why do you think so? (Try the words sound, vibrate, and string.)
grade2.li.1: A long piece of string or yarn (a few big steps long)
grade2.li.2: A pencil or a paper clip to help poke a small hole and hold the string
grade2.li.4: Ask: How can I send my voice to a friend across the room?
grade2.li.5: Imagine: How will the sound travel? (Along the string!)
grade2.li.6: Plan: Poke a small hole in the bottom of each cup for the string.
grade2.li.7: Build: Thread the string through both cups and tie a knot or use a paper clip inside so it stays.
grade2.li.8: Test: Walk apart until the string is tight. One person talks into a cup while the other listens.
grade2.li.9: Make it better: Try it with the string loose, then tight. Which one works better?
grade2.teks.0: (Grade 2 scientists to meet: Alexander Graham Bell, Marie Daly, Mario Molina, Jane Goodall.)

grade3.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade3.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Blast Off! breakout. Build a moving model that shows the Moon orbiting the Earth while the Earth orbits the Sun.
grade3.footer: Grade 3 Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade3.p.0: How can you model the way objects move in space? Build a model that shows the Moon going around the Earth, and the Earth going around the Sun. A good model helps you explain what you cannot see all at once.
grade3.p.1: What does your model show well?
grade3.p.2: What can't your model show? (Try the words orbit, model, and far.)
grade3.li.0: 3 balls of different sizes (big = Sun, medium = Earth, small = Moon) — or paper circles
grade3.li.1: 2 craft sticks, straws, or pencils to hold the Earth and Moon
grade3.li.2: Tape, and a little clay or a paper plate for the Sun in the middle
grade3.li.3: Ask: How can I show the Moon orbiting Earth and Earth orbiting the Sun?
grade3.li.4: Imagine: Which ball is the Sun? Where do the Earth and Moon go?
grade3.li.5: Plan: Decide how the Earth will move around the Sun, and how the Moon will move around the Earth.
grade3.li.6: Build: Put the big "Sun" ball in the middle. Attach the "Earth" so it can circle the Sun, and the "Moon" so it can circle the Earth.
grade3.li.7: Test: Move your model. Does the Earth go around the Sun? Does the Moon go around the Earth at the same time?
grade3.li.8: Make it better: Fix anything that moves the wrong way, then show a friend.
grade3.teks.0: (Grade 3 innovators to explore: scientists who study space and design rockets.)

grade4.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade4.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Light It Up! breakout. Wire a battery, a wire, and a bulb into a working circuit — then test what happens with a gap, and which materials conduct.
grade4.footer: Grade 4 Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade4.p.0: How can you make a small bulb light up? Build a closed circuit so electricity flows from the battery, through the wire, to the bulb, and back. Then break the loop and see what happens.
grade4.p.1: What had to be true for the bulb to light?
grade4.p.2: Which materials were conductors, and which were insulators? (Try the words circuit, closed path, and conductor.)
grade4.li.0: 1 battery (a D-cell works well) and a battery holder if you have one
grade4.li.1: 1 small bulb (and a bulb holder) or an LED
grade4.li.2: 2–3 wires with the ends stripped (or aluminum foil strips)
grade4.li.3: Test materials: a paper clip, a coin, a rubber band, a plastic spoon, a pencil
grade4.li.4: Ask: How do I make the bulb light up?
grade4.li.5: Imagine: Draw the loop — battery, wire, bulb, and back to the battery.
grade4.li.6: Plan: Decide how the wires will connect the battery to the bulb.
grade4.li.7: Build: Connect it into a full loop with no gaps. Watch the bulb light!
grade4.li.8: Test: Now open the loop (pull one wire loose). Does the bulb go out? Then close it again.
grade4.li.9: Make it better: Put each test material into the gap. Which ones let the bulb light (conductors) and which don't (insulators)?
grade4.teks.0: (Grade 4 innovators to explore: engineers who design electronics and clean energy.)

grade5.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade5.lead: A hands-on STEM buddy for the Round and Round breakout. Track a shadow across the day to watch Earth's spin at work — then use it to tell time like an ancient sundial.
grade5.footer: Grade 5 Science · Critical Thinking Online Breakouts · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade5.p.0: Can you use a shadow to tell time? As Earth spins, the Sun appears to move, so shadows move and change length. Build a shadow tracker that marks the shadow each hour — then read the time from it.
grade5.p.1: When was the shadow longest, and when was it shortest?
grade5.p.2: Why did the shadow move? (Try the words rotate, spin, and shadow.)
grade5.li.0: A stick, pencil, or straw stood straight up (the "gnomon")
grade5.li.1: A flat spot in the sun, or a paper plate with the stick through the center
grade5.li.2: Chalk or a marker to mark the shadow, and a clock to check the time
grade5.li.3: A sunny day and a spot the stick won't be moved
grade5.li.4: Ask: How does a shadow change through the day?
grade5.li.5: Imagine: Predict — will the shadow be longer in the morning or at noon?
grade5.li.6: Plan: Choose a spot where the stick stays still all day.
grade5.li.7: Build: Stand the stick straight up so it makes a clear shadow.
grade5.li.8: Test: Mark the tip of the shadow every hour and write the time next to it.
grade5.li.9: Make it better: Use your marks as a sundial — can a friend read the time from the shadow? Fix any marks that are hard to read.
grade5.teks.0: (Grade 5 innovators to explore: scientists who study Earth, sky, and time.)

grade6.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade6.lead: A hands-on STEM companion to the Cargo Ship Rescue breakout. Turn the density idea from Lock 2 into a real engineering test — then improve your design like a marine engineer.
grade6.footer: Science Critical Thinking Breakouts · Grade 6 · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade6.p.0: The Port of Houston needs a barge that carries the most cargo without sinking. Using a single square of aluminum foil, design and build a barge hull that holds the greatest number of pennies before it sinks or takes on water. Then redesign to beat your own record.
grade6.p.1: Claim — What hull shape carried the most cargo?
grade6.p.2: Evidence — What did your two trials show?
grade6.p.3: Reasoning — Use the words mass, volume, and density to explain why. (A wider, deeper hull holds more mass in more volume, so the barge's overall density stays below the water's — and it floats.)
grade6.li.0: 2 squares of aluminum foil, 15 cm × 15 cm (one per build round)
grade6.li.1: A tub, sink, or large bowl of water
grade6.li.3: Paper towels, a ruler, and this recording sheet
grade6.li.4: Optional: a small amount of tape
grade6.li.5: Define the problem: carry the most pennies on a foil barge without sinking.
grade6.li.6: Imagine & brainstorm: sketch two hull ideas. Which spreads the mass over the most volume — a flat raft, or a hull with tall walls?
grade6.li.7: Plan: choose one design, measure your hull, and predict a penny count.
grade6.li.8: Create: build your barge from one foil square. Seal any gaps.
grade6.li.9: Test: float it, then add pennies one at a time, spread evenly, until it sinks. Record the last count that stayed afloat.
grade6.li.10: Improve: redesign with the second foil square to beat Round 1. Change one thing (wall height, width, penny placement) so you know what helped.
grade6.teks.0: (Labor data: O*NET & the Texas Workforce Commission; 6.4(C) investigate STEM careers.)

grade7.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade7.lead: A hands-on STEM companion to the Rescue Run breakout. Turn the thermal-equilibrium idea from Lock 4 into a real test — design an insulated container, then graph how it cools and read the slope like the drone's motion graph.
grade7.footer: Science Critical Thinking Breakouts · Grade 7 · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade7.p.0: The rescue team's medicine must stay cold in the desert sun. Using common materials, design an insulated container that keeps an ice cube frozen the longest (or keeps cold water coldest over 15 minutes). Then redesign to beat your own record.
grade7.p.1: Claim — Which design kept the cargo cold the longest?
grade7.p.2: Evidence — Compare the slopes of your two graphs.
grade7.p.3: Reasoning — Use heat flows hot→cold, conduction/convection/radiation, and thermal equilibrium to explain why. (Insulation only slows the heat; given enough time, inside and outside still reach the same temperature.)
grade7.li.0: A small cup or container as the "core," plus a larger outer container
grade7.li.1: Insulators to test: cotton balls, foil, bubble wrap, paper towels, felt, foam
grade7.li.2: Ice cubes of equal size (or equal amounts of cold water) as the "medicine"
grade7.li.3: A thermometer (or temperature probe), a timer, tape, this recording sheet
grade7.li.4: Define the problem: keep the cold cargo cold the longest.
grade7.li.5: Imagine & brainstorm: which materials trap the least heat flow? Predict a ranking.
grade7.li.6: Plan: choose your insulation layers and sketch the build.
grade7.li.7: Create: build the cooler around the core; seal gaps that let convection in.
grade7.li.8: Test: record the temperature every 2–3 minutes for ~15 minutes. Keep every team's start temperature and ice size the same (a fair test).
grade7.li.9: Improve: change one variable (add a layer, seal a gap, add a reflective wrap) and retest so you know what helped.
grade7.teks.0: (Labor data: O*NET & the Texas Workforce Commission; 7.4(C) investigate STEM careers.)

grade8.crumb: ‹ Teacher launch · Science Critical Thinking Breakouts
grade8.h1: Reaction in a Bag & Straw Rocket
grade8.lead: A two-part hands-on STEM companion to the Launch Control breakout. Part A proves conservation of mass (Lock 1 & 3). Part B tests Newton's Second Law, a = F ÷ m (Lock 2).
grade8.footer: Science Critical Thinking Breakouts · Grade 8 · Self-contained, no logins, no data collected.
grade8.p.0:
Part A — Fuel check: the launch team must prove that a chemical reaction doesn't lose mass. Design a sealed system that lets a fizzing reaction happen while you measure mass before and after.
Part B — Thrust check: engineers must predict how added cargo changes a rocket's acceleration. Build a straw rocket and test how payload mass changes how far/fast it flies at a fixed launch push.
grade8.p.1: Claim — Was mass conserved? How did payload mass affect the flight?
grade8.p.3: Reasoning — Use atoms rearrange, sealed system, conservation of mass, and a = F ÷ m to explain why. (In a sealed system no atoms leave, so mass is unchanged; with fixed force, more mass means less acceleration.)
grade8.li.0: Part A: a zip-seal bag, baking soda, vinegar, a small cup, a balance/scale
grade8.li.1: Part B: a straw, paper, tape, a slightly wider straw or launcher, paperclips (payload mass), a tape measure
grade8.li.2: This recording sheet and a pencil
grade8.li.3: Define the problem: prove mass is conserved, then test how mass changes acceleration.
grade8.li.4: Imagine & brainstorm: how will you keep the reaction fully sealed? What payloads will you test?
grade8.li.5: Plan: predict the after-reaction mass (Part A) and rank your payloads by expected distance (Part B).
grade8.li.6: Create: build the sealed bag (keep vinegar in the cup until sealed) and the straw rocket.
grade8.li.7: Test: mass the sealed bag before and after the fizz; launch the rocket with 0, 1, and 3 paperclips, measuring distance each time (repeat trials).
grade8.li.8: Improve: if the bag lost mass, find the leak and reseal; refine the rocket fins so only mass is changing between launches (a fair test).
grade8.teks.0: (Labor data: O*NET & the Texas Workforce Commission; 8.4(C) investigate STEM careers.)
